result.summary: After Acheloüs finishes a tale, Ixion's son mocks it, and Lelex answers by telling how Jupiter and Mercury were turned away by a whole village but welcomed by the poor Philemon and Baucis. The gods drown the village, turn the cottage into a temple, and later change the couple into intertwined trees. Acheloüs then turns to the shape-changing Proteus.

scenes.title: Ixion's son scoffs
scenes.summary: The synopsis is given, then the river falls silent and Ixion's son mocks the tale of gods changing forms.
scenes.stakes: Irreverent doubt of the gods' power risks offending them and shaming the host.

scenes.title: Lelex begins: the refused gods
scenes.summary: Lelex says he saw the oak and lime tree in Phrygia. Jupiter and Mercury, disguised, are shut out of a thousand houses but taken in by the poor Baucis and Philemon.
scenes.stakes: The disguised gods need shelter, and the villagers risk divine punishment for their inhospitality.

scenes.title: The humble feast
scenes.summary: Baucis and Philemon prepare a poor but generous meal. The wine refills itself and they try to kill their goose.
scenes.stakes: The old couple fear offending their guests and want to kill their only goose.

scenes.title: Flood and temple
scenes.summary: The gods reveal themselves and lead the couple up the mountain. The village sinks into a marsh and the cottage becomes a temple, and Philemon asks to be priests and to die together.
scenes.stakes: The couple must escape the flood; the village is destroyed.

scenes.title: Two trees
scenes.summary: Baucis and Philemon turn into trees. Lelex says he saw the garlands at Tyana.
scenes.stakes: The couple face death, but they are spared separation.

scenes.title: Acheloüs on Proteus
scenes.summary: Everyone is astonished, and Acheloüs tells Theseus of Proteus and his many forms.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic for Pirithoüs, who is not named in this section.

notable_quotes.reason: Moral of the tale: the pious who worship gods are themselves honoured.
Captures the warmth that outweighs the couple's poverty.
Touching farewell of the couple as they become trees.

analysis.text: The tale rewards hospitality and piety and punishes those who turn strangers away, showing that gods may come in disguise.
Marital devotion is rewarded by a shared death and a shared form.

legacy.text: The story of Baucis and Philemon became a classic image of faithful old age and hospitality, retold by writers such as Swift and Goethe's Faust (1808–1832).

fun_facts.text: The 'Philemon and Baucis' tale is an etiological myth explaining a lake and two neighbouring trees in Phrygia.

language_notes.text: The son of Ixion is Pirithoüs, king of the Lapithae, here a skeptic who scorns the gods.
Pittheus was king of Troezen and father of Aethra, Theseus's mother. Pelops had ruled the land of Pelops (the Peloponnese) before him; Pittheus's father was Pelops.
Coots are dark water birds; cormorants are diving seabirds. Both mark the once-inhabited land as now watery waste.
The grandson of Atlas is Mercury (the Greek Hermes), whose mother Maia was Atlas's daughter. Jupiter calls him his 'parent' loosely here, meaning his son, a confusing wording.
The Caduceus is Mercury's herald's staff, entwined with snakes; his winged cap and sandals are the 'wings' he lays aside.
'Fasten against them' means the doors were barred to keep the strangers out.
Faggots are bundles of sticks bound for firewood; the boiler is a small cooking pot or kettle.
Chine is the backbone cut of the pig, here the cured meat kept for special use.
"Beguile the intervening hours" means they pass the waiting time pleasantly with talk, so it does not seem long.
A potsherd is a broken piece of pottery, used here as a shim to steady the wobbling table.
The berries of chaste Minerva are olives, since the goddess gave the olive tree to Athens. They are "double-tinted" because they are green and black.
The fire "sends up" the meal, meaning the hot dishes are brought from the hearth after a short pause.
Niggardly means stingy or grudging.
"Guardian of their little cottage" says the goose served as a watch animal, as geese were known to raise alarms.
"It" refers to the neighbours' killing of the goose; the gods forbid Baucis and Philemon to kill their only goose, which they had been trying to catch for the guests.
The distance is measured by a bowshot: as far as an arrow shot once can fly.
Forked stakes were the crude wooden posts that held up the humble cottage; they are replaced by marble columns.
"Enervated" is used in its older sense: weakened, drained of strength.
Tyana was a city in Cappadocia, Asia Minor; Lelex, the speaker, claims local knowledge of these trees.
"The Calydonian river" is Acheloüs, the river-god, whose waters ran in Calydonia; he is the narrator hosting Theseus.
Proteus was a sea-god able to change shape at will; "the sea that embraces the earth" is the ocean thought to encircle the land.

context_notes.text: Acheloüs is a river god who has been telling stories to Theseus and his companions at a feast.
Phrygia was a region of Asia Minor. Lelex describes a real-seeming landmark to give the tale credibility.
Thatched cottages of straw and marsh reeds were the humblest dwellings, signalling the couple's poverty.
The visitors are Jove and Mercury in disguise, testing the hospitality of the locals. The low door forces even gods to stoop.
Sedge is a grass-like marsh plant, dried here for stuffing a cushion. The couch is a dining couch where guests reclined.
Self-refilling wine is the first sign to the couple that their guests are divine.
The son of Saturn is Jove (Jupiter), king of the gods, who is traveling disguised with Mercury to test human hospitality.
Philemon's wish reflects ancient ideals of marriage: to be spared the grief of outliving one's spouse and the burden of burying them.

literary_notes.text: Ovid sketches the scoffer as a despiser of the gods and haughty, signaling that impiety will be contrasted with piety.
Repeating 'a thousand houses' from the previous line stresses how universal the inhospitality is, preparing for the contrast with the one welcoming cottage.
Poverty is made 'light' by acceptance, turning a hardship into a virtue and setting up the couple's reward.
The household's tiny size is humorously presented as a rule-less hierarchy, where the same two persons are both masters and servants.
Detailed domestic actions, such as the old woman's breath kindling the fire, evoke their poverty and care.
The line shows the couple's generosity: their sincere welcome matters more than the meager food and outweighs their poverty.
The old hosts cannot catch the nimble goose, yet it flees to the very gods they are feeding, who will protect it.
Vivid visual detail of yellow thatch, marble and gilded roof shows the miraculous transformation of the poor cottage into a temple.
Their last shared words of farewell as bark covers their faces make the transformation tender rather than frightening.
Lelex closes with a maxim summarizing the tale's lesson: piety is rewarded and the pious become objects of worship themselves.
The repeated "one while... at another... sometimes" pattern builds a rapid catalog that mimics Proteus's ceaseless shifting.
